strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference image with a clothing-change description addresses a limitation of image-only and text-only person retrieval. ITCPR, with 2,202 queries and 20,510 gallery images, is a potentially useful community resource.

The reported improvements over simple fusion are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.549% Rank-1 and 55.260% mAP, versus 32.016% and 41.831% for fine-tuned image-plus-text averaging. Improvements also hold with ViT-B/16.

The two-stage pipeline is understandable and practical. The lightweight mapper, frozen encoders during inversion training, and substantial training and hardware details support reproducibility. The manuscript clearly defines zero-shot as avoiding composed retrieval triplets, while using supervised person data.

The supplementary experiments meaningfully broaden the evidence through loss, data, architecture, fusion, and runtime ablations. Reporting that joint visual/text supervision can underperform text supervision alone provides useful information about the method's limitations.
weaknesses: The principal comparison with prior composed retrieval methods is not adequately controlled. Table 1 explicitly evaluates a Pic2Word mapper trained with original CLIP parameters alongside fine-tuned encoders, introducing a representation mismatch. A mapper retrained with the same encoders and person data is needed. Table 2 provides useful partial controls, but does not establish the headline advantage over a properly adapted Pic2Word; the closely related method in reference [2] is also not evaluated.

Methodological originality is limited. Image-to-pseudo-word mapping and prompt composition closely follow existing zero-shot composed image retrieval, while encoder fine-tuning and the matching losses build on established person-retrieval methods. The strongest original contribution is the task and benchmark; the manuscript should more precisely distinguish its identity-aware and text-supervised adaptation from the existing mechanisms.

Model selection and final evaluation are insufficiently separated. ITCPR is designated exclusively for testing, yet Supplementary C.3-C.5 select architectures and configurations using its reported performance without explaining an independent validation procedure. This leaves selection bias unresolved. Missing repeated runs or uncertainty estimates particularly weaken conclusions about small architecture and ensemble improvements.

The benchmark needs stronger validation. Selecting pairs with partially preserved clothing narrows the tested setting, while aggregate results do not establish performance across source datasets or difficult same-clothing/different-identity distractors. The encoder-assisted gallery re-annotation is sensible, but its encoder, candidate count, annotation agreement, and coverage audit are insufficiently documented to assess residual false negatives. These gaps matter because the benchmark is a central contribution.

The explicit surveillance and public-security motivation requires a substantive discussion of privacy, misuse, and unequal identification errors. The manuscript also does not document permissions and redistribution conditions for the reused person imagery. Public availability alone does not resolve these questions.
